A brake that is still set fights the tug's own force straight through the towbar and the nose gear, and the crew has no way to feel that resistance from the tug's own seat before something in that load path gives.

That skips the steering bypass pin. Without it, the tug's own force is fed straight into the nosewheel's steering linkage every time the tow turns, and that is exactly the load path that bends a steering collar or tears a hydraulic line the crew will not find until the aircraft's own steering fails on a taxi it should never have failed on.

You are standing in the tow path while the aircraft is moving. A jet under tow does not stop for a person the way it would for an obstacle a driver could see coming — the tug operator's own view down the fuselage is already partly blocked, and the tow path is kept clear so that blind spot never has to matter.

title: Read the repair order and the lift points
instruction: Check the job, the bus's lift-point diagram, its weight and the HV disable procedure for this model.
rationale: Every model lifts at different frame points and disables its high-voltage system a different way — a point that is correct on a diesel cousin can be sheet metal on this one. The diagram and the disable procedure for this specific bus are read before anything is touched.

title: Disable the high-voltage system
instruction: Master switch off, then pull the HV service disconnect and pocket it.
rationale: The service disconnect opens the traction battery circuit itself, not just the low-voltage control loop the master switch runs. It is pulled after the master switch, in that order, and it stays in your pocket so nobody can reinsert it while you are underneath a bus you believe is de-energised.

title: Prove the HV bus is de-energised
instruction: Wait the discharge time, then read the HV bus at the test point with the CAT III meter and commit inside the safe band.
rationale: The traction battery's capacitors hold a lethal charge for a period after the disconnect is pulled, following the same live-dead-live discipline NFPA 70E requires of any electrical energy source. The meter, read only after the full wait, is the actual proof the orange cables are safe to touch.

title: Chock the wheels
instruction: Chocks both sides of a wheel at each axle, parking brake set.
rationale: The bus must not roll on the lift pads during the first few inches of travel, when the columns have barely started to take the load and the pads have the least purchase on the frame. Chocks at both axles and the parking brake set before any column moves at all.

title: Place the lift pads on the frame points
instruction: Roll each column in and set the pad under the frame lift point from the diagram.
rationale: The frame lift point is engineered by the manufacturer to carry the full weight of an 18-tonne bus; nothing else along that frame or body is. The pad goes exactly on the marked point, on every column, with no column left to guesswork.

title: Raise in sync
instruction: Raise all columns together, watching the level — stop and correct if one column leads.
rationale: Four columns raising even slightly unevenly twist the bus's frame and shift its whole load onto only two of the four pads. The controller works to sync them, but the technician watches the level readout the entire climb and stops the raise the moment one column leads.

title: Lower onto the mechanical locks
instruction: Engage the locks on every column and lower the bus onto them until the hydraulics are unloaded.
rationale: The bus is worked under only once it is resting on its mechanical locks, not on the columns' hydraulic rams. Lowering onto the locks takes the load off the hydraulics entirely, so a seal or a hose failure afterward has nothing left under it to drop.

title: Work under the bus
instruction: With the bus on its locks and HV proven off, disconnect the drive motor.
rationale: Everything before this step — HV proven dead, chocks set, pads on the frame, locks engaged — is what turns pulling a drive motor from underneath an 18-tonne bus into an ordinary task instead of a gamble.

title: Inspect under the bus while it is up
instruction: Look over the HV harness, the air lines and the frame while you have the access, and click the defect.
rationale: A bus sits up on locks with clear access underneath for maybe an hour a month, and that hour is the only chance anyone gets to actually see the underside. What gets caught now is what keeps this bus out of the shop again next month.

title: Clear the bay and lower
instruction: Everyone and everything out from under, locks released together, lower to the floor, reinsert the service disconnect last.
rationale: The lower is called only by the person who has personally looked underneath the bus and confirmed the bay is clear of hands, tools and feet. The service disconnect goes back in only once the bus is back down on the ground and the job is fully closed.

situation: A tech from the next bay has walked up with a diagnostic scanner, doesn't see your lock and tag, and is reaching for the master switch to bring the bus back up.
instruction: Stop them before that switch moves — this bus is not back together yet.
missed: The other tech flipped the master switch while you were reaching for a chock. It did not re-energise the HV bus by itself — the service disconnect was already pulled — but it proved the lock and tag alone were not stopping anyone's hand.

situation: Column 3's pad has started to walk outward on the frame rail as the load comes on — old grease at that lift point is letting it slide instead of sitting still.
instruction: Stop the raise and reseat that pad before it climbs any further off the marked point.
missed: The raise continued while column 3's pad kept walking off the lift point. By the time the bus reached working height, that corner was resting on the edge of the frame rail rather than square on the point it was engineered for.

explanation: You touched the orange high-voltage cable with bare hands before the system was disabled and proven. The traction battery is 600 V and does not care that the bus is switched off.
You put a lift pad on the body skirt instead of the frame lift point. The skirt is sheet metal; it crushes, the bus shifts on the columns, and it comes down where it likes.
You started the raise with the wheels unchocked and the bus in neutral. A bus that rolls on the pads as it lifts rolls off them.

You went under the bus with the columns still on hydraulics, locks not engaged. A seal, a hose or a valve is all that is holding 18 tonnes over you; the mechanical locks are what a person works under.

title: Read the fuel lane board: lane, spill plan and shutoff
instruction: Read the lane board: which lane, the fuelling rules, where the emergency fuel shutoff is, where the spill kit is, and the brake check the coach needs tonight.
rationale: The fuel lane is the one part of the yard where diesel, moving coaches and people on foot all meet, and its rules are posted because they have to be known before they are needed: engine off, nozzle attended, where the emergency fuel shutoff is and what the spill plan says. The coach's paperwork on the board also says what check it is due — a coach that needs its brakes looked at tonight is a coach that does not go out tomorrow if it fails.

title: Set the parking brake, then engine off and key out
instruction: Pull the parking brake valve, then shut the engine down and take the key out before anyone touches the filler.
rationale: A coach in the fuel lane is secured in a fixed order: the parking brake set while the engine and air are still up, then the engine off and the key in the worker's pocket, so the coach cannot be started or driven while its tank is open and someone is at its side. A running engine at the island is heat and electricity next to diesel vapour, and a key left in is an invitation to the next person aboard.

title: Chock the coach's wheels
instruction: Set the wheel chock tight against the rear drive wheel on the downhill side.
rationale: The brake check coming up deliberately releases the parking brakes and drains the air, and a coach on even a slight grade will roll when it does. The chock goes against the drive wheel on the downhill side before the check starts and before anyone goes near the wheels or under the coach, because it is the only thing holding the coach once the air is gone.

title: Fill the tank with a hand on the nozzle
instruction: Put the diesel nozzle in the green-capped filler and hold the trigger through the fill — no latch, eyes on the filler, until it clicks off.
rationale: The fill is attended because the automatic shutoff that stops the pump at a full tank is a backup, not a plan — it can fail, the nozzle can slip out, and the first sign of either is diesel on the pavement. A hand on the nozzle and eyes on the filler means the person fuelling is the shutoff. The safety data sheet for diesel, which HazCom puts at the island, is the reason vapour and skin contact are kept to the minimum the job needs.

title: Top up the DEF from its own blue-capped filler
instruction: Take the blue DEF nozzle to the blue-capped DEF filler only, and top up the tank.
rationale: Diesel exhaust fluid is what the coach's exhaust treatment uses to clean up its emissions, and it lives in its own tank behind its own blue cap. The two fillers sit side by side on many coaches, which is why the nozzles, caps and filler necks are different colours and sizes — and why the fueller reads the cap, not the position, before a nozzle goes in.

title: Put the fuel cap back on to the click
instruction: Nozzle back in the holster, then turn the diesel cap on until it clicks and close the filler door.
rationale: A diesel cap that is not turned to its click lets fuel slosh out on the first corner and lets water in on the first wash, and a cap left on the island is a coach running with an open tank. The nozzle goes back into its holster first, so the next person does not drive over a hose, and the cap is turned until it clicks because the click is the cap's seal seating.

title: Walk round the coach for leaks and damage
instruction: Walk the coach: fluid under the engine and the axles, the tyres, the lights and the body, before the brake check.
rationale: The walk-round at the end of the day is when a coach's small faults are found while there is still a night to fix them: a coolant puddle under the engine bay, a tyre gone soft, a light out. The report the driver and the yard write depends on someone actually looking, and a puddle under a parked coach is the easiest fault in the yard to find and the most expensive one to find on the road.

title: Build the air and read governor cut-out
instruction: Start the engine, build air pressure and commit the reading where the governor cuts the compressor out, against the coach maker's figure.
rationale: The air brake check starts from a known point: the compressor builds pressure until the governor cuts it out at the figure the coach maker sets, and a governor cutting out too low leaves less air than the brakes were designed around, while one that never cuts out is about to cook a compressor. The reading is taken at the moment the compressor unloads, because that is the governor's setting — not a number on the way up.

title: Hold a full brake application and watch the leak-down
instruction: Engine off, parking brake released on the chocks: press and hold a full application steady, and watch the gauge for a minute after the first drop.
rationale: The applied leakage test is how the brake system's leaks show: with the engine off and a full application held steady, the pressure is allowed its first drop as the chambers fill and then watched for a minute, and a system losing more than the state CDL manual's limit has a leak that will empty the tanks. The application is held steady because a foot that pumps the pedal is spending air, and the test is measuring the air the system loses on its own.

title: Fan the air down and prove the low-air warning
instruction: Fan the brake pedal to bleed the air down and confirm the low-air warning lamp and buzzer come on before the pressure falls below the manual's figure.
rationale: The low-air warning is what tells a driver the brakes are running out of air while there is still enough to stop, and 49 CFR 393 requires coaches with air brakes to have one. It is proven by fanning the pressure down and watching for the lamp and buzzer to come on before the figure in the state CDL manual, because a warning that comes on too late is a warning that arrives with the spring brakes.

title: Measure the pushrod stroke against its limit
instruction: With a full application held by your crew mate, measure the pushrod's travel at the rear brake chamber and commit it against the chamber's readjustment limit.
rationale: An air brake's stroke grows as its linings wear, and past the readjustment limit for its chamber size the brake reaches the end of its travel before it is fully applied — it looks fine and stops badly. CVSA's out-of-service criteria count brakes past that limit, and a coach with enough of them is off the road. The stroke is measured with a full application held, from the same mark each time, because that is the only reading the limit means anything against.

title: Look along the air lines at the axles
instruction: With the coach chocked, look along the air lines and brake hoses at the axles: chafing, cracking, kinks, and anything rubbing.
rationale: An air line that rubs on a bracket with every bump wears through a layer at a time, and the first sign of failure on the road is a brake that stops working and a pressure that falls. The coach is chocked before anyone looks underneath, and the lines are traced along their whole run to the chambers, because the chafe is always where the line touches something the fitter did not expect it to touch.

title: Tag the coach out of service and lock the key away
instruction: Hang the out-of-service tag on the steering wheel and put the key in the shop lock box, so the coach cannot go out in the morning.
rationale: A chafed air line is a defect that affects safe operation, and 49 CFR 396 has it repaired before the coach runs again — which in a yard that sends coaches out before the day shift arrives means the coach has to be physically stopped from going out, not just written up. The tag on the wheel tells the morning driver, and the key in the shop's lock box makes sure the tag is obeyed.

title: Write the inspection report for the shop and the morning
instruction: Record the fuel and DEF, the coolant leak, the brake check readings, the pushrod stroke, and the chafed air line with the coach tagged out.
rationale: The driver vehicle inspection report is the carrier's record under 49 CFR 396 of what was found and what was fixed, and the mechanic who works on the coach tonight starts from it. A defect that is not on the report is a defect the shop does not know to fix, and the report is also what the next driver reviews and signs before taking the coach — written now, at the coach, it says what is actually wrong with it.

title: Check in with the yard dispatcher and the hostler
instruction: Call the yard dispatcher: the coach is fuelled and tagged out with a chafed air line, and check in with the hostler after the backing in the lane.
rationale: Dispatch builds tomorrow's pull-out from this call, so a coach that will not be ready is known now rather than at five in the morning. It is also the crew's check-in: a coach backing into a lane where someone is holding a brake pedal is the near miss the hostler and the service worker will both remember, and the union's practice is to say so on the radio and name the member assistance line alongside it.

situation: At the next island a coach has pulled away with the nozzle still in its filler — the hose has snapped off and diesel is pouring across the lane.
instruction: Hit the emergency fuel shutoff on its post — every dispenser in the lane stops at once.
missed: The dispenser kept pumping through the broken hose; diesel spread across two lanes and into the drain before the yard supervisor ran to the shutoff, and a coach pulling in slid through the edge of it.

situation: The yard hostler is backing another coach into the lane behind you, reverse alarm going, with nobody spotting and you at the rear wheels.
instruction: Call the hostler on the yard radio to stop — you are in the lane behind the coach.
missed: The backing coach stopped a metre from the rear of the coach under test only because the hostler happened to check a mirror; the service worker at the wheel never saw it coming.

explanation: You lifted the DEF nozzle toward the diesel filler. Diesel exhaust fluid in a diesel tank does not burn — it crystallises in the fuel system and can wreck the pumps and injectors, and a coach that leaves the yard with it will fail on the road. The fillers are colour-coded and sized differently for this reason, and each nozzle goes only into its own filler.

You went to start fuelling with the coach's engine still idling. A running engine is a hot exhaust and a live electrical system a metre from a tank breathing diesel vapour, and a coach left running in a fuel lane can be knocked into gear by anyone climbing aboard. The engine goes off and the key comes out before the cap comes off, every time.

You clicked the nozzle's hold-open latch and turned to walk off. A latched nozzle fills until its automatic shutoff trips — if it trips — and the person who latched it is somewhere else when the tank overflows, the nozzle falls out or someone drives off with it in the filler. The fill is attended with a hand on the nozzle from start to finish.

You went to look under the coach before the wheels were chocked. A parked coach with a leaking air system can lose its brakes as the pressure drops, and during a brake check the parking brakes are deliberately released — nobody goes under or in front of a coach during a brake check, and nobody goes under at all until it is chocked.

title: Pull the decompression checklist
instruction: Open the rapid decompression and emergency descent checklist immediately.
rationale: This is the one checklist a crew member has the least time to think through from memory — pulling it and running it in order is what keeps every step in the sequence the airline actually trained for, not whatever comes to mind first under pressure.

title: Secure your own mask first
instruction: Put on your own oxygen mask and confirm flow before doing anything else.
rationale: A crew member who cannot think clearly is a crew member who cannot help anyone, and the only way to stay useful to this whole cabin is securing your own oxygen before turning to help with a single other row.

title: Announce the descent, then confirm the sign
instruction: Make the emergency descent PA per the checklist, then confirm the seatbelt sign is illuminated.
rationale: Passengers need to hear what's happening from this crew's own voice before anything else, and confirming the sign right after is what makes sure the instruction to stay seated is actually backed up by the cabin's own visible signal.

title: Sweep the cabin for what's wrong
instruction: Two things in this cabin aren't right for the descent. Find them once your own mask is already on.
rationale: This sweep only starts once this crew member's own mask is secure — everything it catches, from a compartment that never dropped to an object still loose on a tray table, is a real hazard to whoever is sitting near it for the rest of the descent.

title: Bring the portable bottle to the failed row
instruction: Carry the portable oxygen bottle to the row whose compartment never dropped.
rationale: A row with no working mask has no oxygen at all until this crew physically brings a portable bottle to it — this happens the moment the failed compartment is found, not after the rest of the sweep is finished.

title: Hold the mask in place and confirm flow
instruction: Hold the portable mask to the passenger's face and confirm oxygen is actually flowing.
rationale: A mask held loosely against someone's face who cannot secure it themselves right now delivers nothing — holding it firmly in place long enough to actually confirm flow is the only way to know this row is getting oxygen at all.

title: Open the backup oxygen cylinder
instruction: Turn the backup cylinder's valve open per its own placard.
rationale: The backup cylinder is what this crew reaches for once the fixed system alone isn't covering every row that needs it, and opening it correctly is a mechanical step the placard spells out, not a judgment call about how much any one passenger needs.

title: Read the backup cylinder's pressure
instruction: Check the pressure gauge before relying on the backup cylinder for the rest of the descent.
rationale: A backup cylinder this crew is about to depend on for the rest of the descent needs its pressure actually confirmed, not assumed from how full it looked in the bracket.

title: Watch the cabin altitude come back down
instruction: Keep an eye on the cabin altitude readout until it settles back into the normal band.
rationale: The decision to stand up and move through this cabin again rests on the cabin altitude actually reading normal, not on how the descent felt — watching it settle is what turns a guess into a confirmed fact.

title: Help the unassisted child
instruction: Now that your own mask is secure, help the child whose mask isn't on.
rationale: This is exactly the help this crew's own mask being secured first was for — a child who needs a hand gets one now, from a crew member who can actually think clearly enough to give it safely.

title: Confirm the cabin is repressurized
instruction: Read the pressure gauge and confirm the cabin has actually returned to a safe reading before standing passengers down from oxygen.
rationale: Passengers come off their masks only once this crew has an actual confirmed reading that the cabin is safe again — not once the descent feels like it's over, which is a guess this checklist has no use for.

title: Sweep the cabin and check on passengers
instruction: Walk the aisle, check on every row, and note anything that still needs attention.
rationale: A cabin that just went through a rapid decompression has people who are shaken, some who may be hurt, and equipment that needs resetting — this walk-through is what actually finds out which of those apply, row by row, instead of assuming everyone is fine because the drill is technically over.

title: Log the event
instruction: Record the sequence, the times, and anything found during the sweep.
rationale: This log is what the airline reviews afterward to confirm the equipment performed and the checklist was followed — a decompression handled perfectly but never logged leaves nothing behind to prove either one.

situation: A second overhead compartment across the aisle also never dropped its mask.
instruction: That row needs the manual release pulled right now.
missed: The second failed compartment sat undiscovered while attention stayed on the first row. That's a whole row still without oxygen.

situation: A passenger starts unbuckling to go help a family member two rows away during the descent.
instruction: That gets a firm stay-seated instruction, not a debate.
missed: The passenger unbuckled and started moving through the cabin mid-descent. That's exactly the fall risk this instruction exists to prevent.

explanation: That child's mask is hanging by their seat, not on their face. A child this age cannot always manage the mask alone even after the adult beside them has theirs on — this is exactly the row this crew's sweep exists to catch once their own mask is already secure.

That laptop is still sitting open on the tray table. Anything not stowed becomes exactly what physics makes it the instant this aircraft pitches hard, and a heavy object flying loose in a cabin full of people reaching for their own masks is its own injury waiting to happen.

That overhead compartment never dropped its mask. A compartment that stays shut is not a row that's fine — it's a row that needs the manual release pulled and, if that fails, a portable bottle brought to it directly.

That's a crew member reaching to help a passenger with their own mask still hanging unused. Every briefing says it for a reason: a crew member who passes out from hypoxia while helping someone else's row is one more person who now needs help, not one less problem in this cabin.

title: Pull the medical event procedure
instruction: Open the airline's own in-flight medical event procedure before doing anything else.
rationale: This procedure is what the airline has actually trained for this exact situation — working from it instead of instinct is what keeps every step that follows in the order the airline itself decided works, rather than whatever feels most urgent in the moment.

title: Call for medical help
instruction: Make the PA call for a medical professional onboard, per the airline's procedure.
rationale: A doctor, nurse or paramedic already on this flight is qualified help that is faster than anything that can be arranged from the ground, and the call goes out immediately, before anything else, because every minute it waits is a minute that qualified help wasn't looking for the row.

title: Notify the captain, then start the timer
instruction: Notify the flight deck a medical event is underway, then start timing it.
rationale: The captain's own decision about whether this flight diverts rests on being told early, not caught up later, and starting the timer right after is what turns "it felt like a while" into an actual number the responding professional and the ground-based support can both use.

title: Clear the path to the row
instruction: Two things near this row are in the way of a fast response. Find them.
rationale: A response is only as fast as the slowest thing standing between the kit and the passenger, and this scan is what catches the obstacles worth thirty seconds each before they cost more than that.

title: Bring the medical kit to the row
instruction: Carry the medical kit to the passenger's row so it's ready the moment a responder needs it.
rationale: The kit staged at the row is the kit that's actually there the instant the responder asks for it — a kit still sitting in the galley is a kit that costs precious seconds the moment it's actually needed.

title: Clear space around the passenger
instruction: Raise the armrest and lay the seatback flat so a responder actually has room to work.
rationale: A responder kneeling in a normal economy row has almost no room to begin with, and clearing what little space this seat can give up is the difference between them actually being able to help and being boxed in by furniture the whole time.

title: Confirm the AED is standing by
instruction: Locate the AED and bring it near, standing by for the responder — never opened or used without one.
rationale: The AED goes to the row and stays ready in a responder's hands, not this crew's own — bringing it near and confirming it's actually functional is the job here, and using it is a decision that belongs entirely to whoever is qualified to make it.

title: Open the portable oxygen bottle
instruction: Turn the valve to open per the bottle's own placard, and hand it to the responder.
rationale: Opening this bottle is a mechanical step this checklist actually spells out, not a decision about whether or how much oxygen this passenger needs — that call, like every clinical one, belongs to whoever is qualified to make it.

title: Read the oxygen bottle's pressure
instruction: Check the pressure gauge before handing the bottle off, and report the reading.
rationale: A responder trusting this bottle has enough oxygen to work with needs that confirmed before it's in their hands, not discovered partway through — reading the gauge and reporting the number is the whole of this crew's job here.

title: Hold the line open to ground medical support
instruction: Hold the relay open and pass along exactly what the responder reports — nothing added, nothing guessed.
rationale: Ground-based medical support is trained to work from exactly what's actually reported, not from this crew's own read on how serious it looks — holding the line open and relaying only what the responder actually says is what keeps that advice grounded in real information.

title: Keep the area clear and private
instruction: Draw the privacy curtain and keep other passengers back from the row.
rationale: A crowd of bystanders costs the responder both room and air, and it costs the passenger whatever dignity is left them in the middle of this — keeping the area clear and private is a real part of the job here, not a courtesy on top of it.

title: Log the event timeline
instruction: Record what was done and when, exactly as it happened — no clinical interpretation.
rationale: This log is a timeline of actions and times, not a diagnosis — it's what the responding professional, the ground-based support and, if it comes to it, the airline and any following care all read afterward, and it only holds up if it says exactly what happened rather than what this crew guessed was going on.

title: Brief the flight deck for a possible diversion
instruction: Report the current status to the captain so the diversion decision — if there is one — is theirs to make with real information.
rationale: Whether this flight diverts is entirely the captain's call, resting on the flight deck's own read of fuel, weather and the airport options available — this crew's job is making sure that call is made with an accurate, current report, not making the call itself.

situation: A passenger two rows back stands up, visibly anxious, and starts asking loudly what's happening.
instruction: That gets redirected and kept back, not explained to at length mid-response.
missed: The anxious passenger kept crowding the aisle, unaddressed, while the response tried to work around them. A second person now needs managing on top of the first.

situation: The responding professional asks this crew whether the passenger should take something from their own bag of medication.
instruction: That question goes to ground medical support, not to a guess from this crew.
missed: The question about medication went unanswered while the response moved on. An unrelayed clinical question is a decision nobody qualified ever actually got to make.

explanation: That AED's pad-expiry indicator reads past due. An AED with expired pads is exactly the piece of equipment this crew needs to already know about before the moment it's actually needed, not discover mid-response.

That cart is still parked square across the aisle to this row. Nothing gets in the way of reaching a passenger who needs help — the path stays clear the entire time this response is running, not just once someone remembers to check.

That is someone offering the passenger their own personal medication. A flight attendant never hands over anyone's personal medication or guesses at what this passenger needs — that call belongs to the responding medical professional or to the ground-based medical support on the line, never to whoever happens to be standing closest with a pill bottle.

That spilled drink is sitting right where the responder is about to kneel. A slip right next to the person already being helped turns one problem into two, and it gets wiped up before anyone's foot finds it, not after.

title: Pull the cabin safety checklist
instruction: Open today's cabin safety checklist before touching anything else.
rationale: The checklist is what turns a walk down the aisle into a check somebody can actually be held to afterward — starting from memory instead of the card is exactly how a step quietly gets skipped without anyone noticing until it matters.

title: Scan the cabin before boarding
instruction: Two things about this cabin aren't right yet. Find them before the first passenger boards.
rationale: This scan happens before boarding for a reason: everything it catches is free to fix right now and expensive to discover once the cabin is full of people and the door is already being armed.

title: Count the emergency equipment
instruction: Verify each item on the placard against what's actually mounted in the cabin.
rationale: The placard names exactly what has to be in this cabin and where, and counting each item against it is the only way to know all of it is actually there rather than assumed present because it usually is.

title: Test the flashlight
instruction: Hold the test button and confirm the flashlight actually lights.
rationale: A flashlight that looks fine in its bracket and a flashlight that actually lights are two different facts, and the only way to know the second one is true is to press the button and watch it happen, not take the first one on faith.

title: Confirm the portable oxygen bottle
instruction: Turn the valve indicator to read the bottle's pressure against the placard's full mark.
rationale: A portable oxygen bottle reads full or it doesn't, and there is no partial credit for a bottle that looks stowed correctly but was never actually checked against its own gauge before the cabin was declared ready.

title: Watch the cabin temperature settle
instruction: Keep an eye on the cabin temperature readout until it settles in the comfort band before boarding.
rationale: A cabin that boards too hot or too cold turns into a stream of individual requests the moment people are seated with nowhere else to go — catching it on the ground, before a single passenger is aboard, is the only point it is still a two-minute fix.

title: Stage the safety demonstration kit
instruction: Bring the demonstration life vest and seatbelt to the briefing seat.
rationale: The demonstration kit staged at the briefing seat now is the kit that is actually ready when the safety briefing starts, rather than something still being dug out of a bin while passengers are already watching.

title: Brief the exit row
instruction: Confirm the exit-row passengers meet the criteria on the briefing card and are willing and able to assist.
rationale: An exit row is only worth what the people sitting in it are actually able and willing to do, and that gets confirmed by asking, out loud, before departure — never assumed from how capable someone happens to look.

title: Arm the door
instruction: Move the door's arming lever to the armed position per the checklist.
rationale: An armed door is what turns the slide into an evacuation slide the instant that door opens — a door left in the disarmed position at the gate is exactly correct for boarding and exactly wrong for the sequence this checklist is about to move into.

title: Cross-check with the door across the aisle
instruction: Hold the cross-check confirmation while the crew member at the opposite door verifies both doors together.
rationale: One person confirming their own work is one person who can miss their own mistake — holding the confirmation open long enough for the crew member across the aisle to actually check the same door from outside your own blind spot is what a cross-check catches that a solo, instant tap never would.

title: Confirm the reseated passenger
instruction: Re-brief whoever is now sitting in the exit row before the door sequence continues.
rationale: An exit-row seat that changes hands resets the briefing to zero — the new passenger's own willingness and ability get confirmed the same way the first one's did, not carried over from a conversation they were never part of.

title: Log the cabin secure
instruction: Hold to confirm and save the log entry — the checklist, the door status and the equipment count together.
rationale: The log is the only record that this specific check happened on this specific flight — a cabin that was actually checked perfectly but never logged leaves nothing behind for anyone downstream to point to.

title: Notify the flight deck
instruction: Call the flight deck on the interphone and report the cabin secure for departure.
rationale: The flight deck's own decision to push back rests in part on hearing this call — a cabin that is actually ready but never reported ready is, from the flight deck's own seat, indistinguishable from a cabin that isn't.

situation: A gate agent hands a last-minute bag through the door right after the cross-check is confirmed.
instruction: That gets stowed before anything else continues.
missed: The bag sat unstowed while the check moved on around it. An unstowed item at departure is exactly the loose object this whole scan exists to catch.

situation: A passenger asks to swap into the exit row right as the door sequence is underway.
instruction: That swap has to be re-briefed before it's approved.
missed: The swap went ahead unbriefed. Whoever is sitting in that exit row now has never once been asked if they can actually do what it needs.

explanation: That carry-on is sitting in the exit-row floor space. An exit row with anything in its own floor space is an exit that does not actually open the way it is supposed to the one time it is ever needed, and this check exists specifically to catch that before the door is ever armed.

That fire extinguisher's inspection tag is past its date. An extinguisher nobody has confirmed still holds pressure is an extinguisher this crew is trusting on faith, and faith is not what the daily equipment check exists to replace.

That flashlight bracket is empty. A flashlight missing from its own bracket is the one item every evacuation checklist calls for by name in a cabin that has just lost its lights, and it gets replaced now, not discovered empty during an actual emergency.

That overhead bin over the exit row is not latched. A bin that lets go in turbulence or a hard landing drops its contents straight into the same aisle an evacuation would need, and a bin over an exit gets checked here for exactly that reason.

title: Pull the evacuation checklist
instruction: Open the airline's own evacuation checklist the instant the command is given.
rationale: This checklist is what turns the command to evacuate into an actual sequence this crew already knows cold — running from it, rather than from memory under pressure, is what keeps every step in the order the airline actually trained for.

title: Look outside before opening
instruction: Look through the door's window and confirm conditions outside before opening it.
rationale: A door opened onto fire, debris or water outside turns a survivable exit into a new hazard — this look is the one thing standing between this crew and finding that out the hard way, and it happens before the handle ever moves.

title: Open the door, then deploy the slide
instruction: Open the door fully, then deploy the evacuation slide.
rationale: The slide only deploys once the door is actually all the way open — trying to move to the slide before that is a step this checklist has no use for, because the mechanism needs the door's own travel to work at all.

title: Confirm the slide is ready
instruction: Confirm the slide is fully inflated and clear before sending anyone onto it.
rationale: A slide that looks deployed and a slide that's actually fully inflated and clear of debris are two different facts — confirming the second one is what this crew is actually staking a passenger's landing on, not the first one alone.

title: Shout the commands, in order, over and over
instruction: Call out the same three commands, loud and repeated, the whole time this door is running.
rationale: Short, repeated, identical commands are what actually cut through a loud, frightened cabin — a passenger who hears the same three words over and over knows exactly what to do without having to think, which is the entire point under these conditions.

title: Scan the flow for what's going wrong
instruction: Two things about this flow aren't right. Find them while people are still moving through the door.
rationale: A flow that looks fine at a glance can still be carrying a bag toward the slide or narrowing around an obstacle nobody's caught yet — this scan is what catches either one while there's still time to fix it before it actually reaches the door.

title: Redirect the passenger with the bag
instruction: Tell the passenger to leave the bag behind, firmly, and keep them moving toward the door.
rationale: This instruction is not a request — a bag heading for the slide gets left behind on this crew's word, immediately, because the next several people in line are the ones who actually pay for it if it isn't.

title: Guide the passenger who's frozen at the sill
instruction: Physically guide the passenger who's stopped moving at the door onto the slide.
rationale: Someone frozen at the sill is not going to talk themselves through it while the line backs up behind them — a firm, direct guide onto the slide is what actually gets them moving again without holding up everyone still coming through this door.

title: Hold the door frame clear
instruction: Stand the door frame and hold position, keeping the flow moving through it the whole time.
rationale: Standing the frame is what keeps this door doing exactly one job — moving people through it as fast as it safely can — instead of becoming a bottleneck the moment this crew member's attention goes somewhere else.

title: Keep the flow rate up
instruction: Watch the flow-rate readout and keep people moving through the door at a steady pace.
rationale: A flow that's too slow leaves people still in a cabin this crew is trying to empty, and a flow that's crowding the sill creates its own fall risk — a steady pace in between is what actually gets the most people out safely in the time available.

title: Read the elapsed time
instruction: Check the evacuation timer against the airline's own benchmark for this door.
rationale: The airline's own benchmark for this door is what this timer is read against, and catching a slow pace early is what actually gives this crew a chance to do something about it, rather than finding out only once the drill is already over.

title: Sweep the cabin one last time
instruction: Do a final visual sweep of the cabin for anyone left before this crew member exits.
rationale: This crew member is the last line between an evacuation that's actually complete and one that quietly left somebody behind — the sweep is what turns "I think everyone's out" into an actual confirmed fact.

title: Exit last, down the slide
instruction: Confirm the cabin is empty, then exit down the slide yourself, last.
rationale: Crew goes down the slide only after every passenger this door was responsible for is already off it — leaving before that confirmed fact is exactly the gap between "probably done" and actually done that this whole drill is built to close.

situation: Another passenger stops dead at the sill, blocking the doorway behind them.
instruction: That gets a firm physical guide onto the slide, right now.
missed: The second frozen passenger sat at the sill while the flow backed up behind them. That's the door stopped again, the same way it already almost did once.

situation: Smoke becomes visible outside the window at this exact door while the flow is still running.
instruction: That door gets redirected to another exit immediately.
missed: People kept coming through this door after smoke was visible outside it. The whole reason conditions get watched, not just checked once, is exactly this kind of change.

explanation: That cart is parked in the doorway itself. Nothing narrows the one path everyone in this section is funneling toward — the doorway stays completely clear the entire time this flow is running.

That passenger is bringing a bag to the door. A bag on a slide punctures it, snags on the way down, or becomes exactly what the next person coming down trips over — it gets left behind before this passenger ever reaches the door, not sorted out once it's already causing a jam.

That door is already being pulled open with nobody having looked through the window first. Opening onto conditions nobody actually checked — fire, debris, water — is exactly the mistake this one look before opening exists to prevent.
That slide has not actually been confirmed inflated and clear. Sending anyone onto a slide nobody has looked at first risks a fall onto a slide that isn't actually ready to take them.

title: Pull the fatigue risk management policy
instruction: Open the airline's own fatigue policy before signing in for duty.
rationale: This policy is what actually defines every threshold this station respects — reading it first is what keeps this self-check honest to the airline's own standard instead of this crew member's own guess at what's probably fine.

title: Complete the alertness self-assessment
instruction: Answer the self-assessment honestly before signing in for duty.
rationale: This self-assessment only protects anyone if it's answered honestly — a crew member who talks themselves into a better answer than the one that's actually true has removed the one check standing between fatigue and a flight this crew member should not have signed in for.

title: Review the factors behind the number
instruction: Review the sleep log and log today's commute time before relying on the self-assessment alone.
rationale: The self-assessment score means more once it's read against what's actually behind it — the sleep log and the commute time are the two facts this crew member has that the score alone doesn't carry on its own.

title: Scan the rest area before using it
instruction: Two things about this rest area aren't right. Find them before trusting it for real rest.
rationale: A rest period only does what it's meant to if the facility it happens in actually supports rest — this scan is what catches the difference between a rest area on paper and one that actually works before this crew member is relying on it.

title: Confirm the rest facility is ready
instruction: Confirm the bunk, the curtain and the temperature are all actually set for rest.
rationale: Confirming this now, before lying down, is what turns a facility that's merely available into one this crew member can actually count on for the rest period it's meant to provide.

title: Test the wake alarm
instruction: Hold the test button and confirm the wake alarm actually sounds before relying on it.
rationale: An alarm that looks set and an alarm that's actually confirmed to sound are two different facts, and the only way to know the second one is true is testing it now, not trusting it for the one moment it actually has to work.

title: Set the rest area temperature
instruction: Turn the dial to a comfortable setting for actual rest, per the facility's own controls.
rationale: A rest period spent too hot or too cold to actually settle into sleep is a rest period that only counted on the schedule, not in practice — setting this now is a small step that makes the difference between the two.

title: Read the fatigue risk indicator
instruction: Check the fatigue risk indicator and read it honestly against the self-assessment already given.
rationale: This indicator exists to be read honestly against the self-assessment this crew member already gave — it only protects anyone if the reading that comes back elevated is actually acted on, not glossed over on the way to signing in.

title: Complete the brief vigilance check
instruction: Keep the vigilance indicator steady in the target band for the whole check.
rationale: A brief, steady vigilance check is a second honest data point alongside the self-assessment — attention that keeps lapsing here is worth noticing now, in a training exercise, rather than for the first time on an actual flight.

title: Call the no-fault fatigue line if needed
instruction: Call the no-fault fatigue reporting line the moment the self-check calls for it — no hesitation.
rationale: This line exists specifically so a genuinely tired crew member can say so without it counting against them — using it the moment it's actually called for is the entire point of building a no-fault system in the first place.

title: Log the duty time
instruction: Record the actual start and end times for this duty period in the logbook.
rationale: An honest, actual-time log is what the airline's own fatigue policy is checked against later — a log that rounds favorably or gets filled in from memory afterward is a log that can no longer be trusted to catch a pattern building over several duty periods.

title: Brief relief crew, then confirm they're alert
instruction: Brief the relief crew member on the handoff, then confirm — honestly — that they're actually alert enough to take over.
rationale: A handoff briefing that skips the honest question about alertness hands off a risk along with the job — confirming it out loud, after the briefing, is what makes this crew member's own honesty about fitness for duty something the next person actually benefits from too.

title: Log the self-check
instruction: Record that the self-check was completed, including anything flagged.
rationale: This log is what lets the airline's own fatigue risk management program see patterns across many crew members over time — a self-check that was actually done but never logged is invisible to the one system built to catch problems this platform, or any one flight, cannot see on its own.

situation: Crew scheduling calls mid-rest asking this crew member to extend today's duty to cover a gap.
instruction: That gets deferred to the fatigue policy, not agreed to on the spot.
missed: The extension got agreed to on the spot, mid-rest, with no reference to the fatigue policy at all. That's the exact pressure this policy was written to take out of one tired crew member's hands.

situation: The primary wake alarm fails to sound as the rest period is ending.
instruction: That's exactly why a backup method exists — use it now.
missed: The failed alarm went unaddressed with no backup used. A single point of failure on something this important is exactly what a backup method exists to catch.

explanation: That rest bunk still has the last crew member's bedding on it. A rest facility that isn't actually reset between users is a rest facility the next tired crew member cannot trust is even clean, let alone quiet enough to actually rest in.

That equipment is running loudly right next to the rest area. A rest period spent next to a noise nobody addressed is not actually rest, whatever the schedule says this crew member was given the time for.

That note says the flight needs covering, so don't call in fatigued. A no-fault fatigue report exists specifically so a genuinely tired crew member can say so without a schedule pressure like this one weighing against it — the pressure is the thing that gets ignored here, not the honest report.
That wake alarm has never actually been tested. A rest period that ends on an alarm nobody confirmed works is a rest period that might not end when this crew member actually needs it to.

title: Brief threats, then confirm roles
instruction: Read the known threats out loud, then confirm who is flying and who is monitoring.
rationale: A threat named out loud is a threat both pilots now actually know about, and confirming roles right after is what makes sure everyone in this flight deck knows exactly whose job is flying and whose is watching, before either one is needed.

title: Scan the flight deck before pushback
instruction: Two things on this flight deck aren't right yet. Find them before the sterile phase begins.
rationale: Everything this scan catches is easy to fix right now and a real gap in this crew's shared picture the moment the sterile phase actually starts and conversation narrows to just what's essential.

title: Confirm the sterile flight deck phase
instruction: Confirm with the other pilot that the flight deck is now sterile, per the checklist's own cue.
rationale: Sterile phase only means something once both pilots have actually agreed it started — confirming it out loud is what turns a rule written in the manual into something this specific flight deck is actually observing right now.

title: Run the checklist, challenge and response
instruction: Call out each checklist item, then confirm the other pilot's response before moving to the next one.
rationale: Challenge-and-response is what makes a checklist a shared, verified fact instead of one pilot's own private assumption — nothing on this list counts as done until it's been called out and answered, every single item.

title: Decline the non-essential conversation
instruction: Decline the non-essential topic and redirect back to the flight, per the sterile-phase rule.
rationale: A conversation about anything that isn't essential to flying this aircraft doesn't belong anywhere in the sterile phase, however harmless it sounds — declining it, every time, is the entire rule, not a judgment call about how distracting this particular topic actually is.

title: Set the altimeter
instruction: Turn the altimeter setting knob to the current setting given, per the checklist.
rationale: Setting the altimeter to the value actually given is a mechanical step this checklist spells out precisely so both pilots' instruments read the same reference — it is never a value this crew estimates or carries over from the last leg.

title: Cross-check both altimeters
instruction: Compare both pilots' altimeter readings and confirm they actually match.
rationale: Two pilots trusting two altimeters that don't actually agree is a disagreement neither one may notice alone — cross-checking them against each other is what catches that gap before it ever becomes the reason either pilot is wrong about where this aircraft actually is.

title: Hold the transmit button for the full readback
instruction: Hold the transmit button through the entire readback — releasing early cuts it off mid-word.
rationale: A readback cut off early is a readback the other party never actually heard in full, and holding the button down for the whole transmission is the only way this crew's own words reliably reach whoever needs them.

title: Hold the approach indicator on target
instruction: Keep the approach indicator centred in the band the whole time you're watching it.
rationale: The pilot monitoring is the second set of eyes this flight deck depends on precisely because the pilot flying is busy flying — holding this indicator on target the whole time is what that monitoring role actually means in practice, not just in title.

title: Call out the deviation
instruction: Speak up immediately the moment you notice anything drifting from what's expected.
rationale: A deviation noticed and not spoken up about might as well not have been noticed at all — CRM only works if the pilot monitoring actually says something the instant something looks wrong, rather than assuming the pilot flying has already seen it too.

title: Acknowledge the callout
instruction: Hold the acknowledgment button through the full readback so the loop actually closes.
rationale: A callout answered with silence has not actually been heard, as far as anyone in this flight deck can tell — holding the acknowledgment through the whole readback is what turns "I said something" into "we both know it now," which is the entire point of saying it in the first place.

title: Confirm the end of the sterile phase
instruction: Confirm, per the checklist's own cue, that the sterile flight-deck phase has ended.
rationale: The sterile phase ends on the same kind of explicit, mutual confirmation it started with — assuming it's over because the workload feels lighter is exactly the kind of guess this procedure was built to replace with an actual agreed fact.

title: Log the CRM debrief
instruction: Record what went well and what to improve before signing off the leg.
rationale: A debrief that never gets written down is a lesson this crew learned once and the next crew never gets to benefit from — logging it is what turns today's flight into something the whole operation can actually learn from.

situation: Air traffic control breaks in with an urgent frequency change mid-checklist.
instruction: That gets handled on the radio panel — the checklist waits.
missed: The urgent frequency change sat unanswered while the checklist continued. An ATC instruction that goes unacknowledged is a instruction this crew cannot assume was ever actually received.

situation: The approach indicator drifts noticeably off target while attention is elsewhere.
instruction: That gets called out immediately, not assumed already seen.
missed: The deviation kept drifting, unspoken, while the crew assumed someone else had already caught it. That assumption is exactly what CRM training exists to break.

explanation: That checklist item was never actually challenged out loud. A silently-skipped item is not the same as a completed one, whatever position the switch happens to be in — challenge-and-response exists specifically so nothing gets assumed done.

That personal phone is out on the console during the sterile phase. Nothing that isn't essential to actually flying the aircraft belongs anywhere in reach during this phase, and a phone sitting there is exactly the kind of distraction the sterile rule exists to remove.

That callout was made and nobody actually answered it. A callout that lands on silence has not actually closed the loop — the other pilot needs to hear it, understand it and say something back, or this crew has no way to know it registered at all.

That weather card was never actually read out during the briefing. A threat that's sitting on the console unbriefed is a threat only one pilot may know about — the whole point of briefing it out loud is making sure it's in both pilots' heads before it ever matters.

title: Pull the galley safety checklist
instruction: Open the galley safety checklist before touching the cart or the cabinets.
rationale: The checklist is what keeps this from turning into whichever steps happen to feel most urgent in the moment — a hot liquid capped out of order is still capped, but a step skipped because the checklist was never opened is a step nobody catches until it costs something.

title: Scan the galley before service
instruction: Two things in this galley aren't secured yet. Find them before the cart moves.
rationale: Everything this scan catches is a five-second fix right now and a real hazard the instant the aircraft moves without warning — that trade only works if the scan actually happens before service starts, not sometime during it.

title: Cap every hot-liquid container
instruction: Cap the coffee pot and the hot water urn before either one leaves the galley.
rationale: A capped container is a container that survives a jolt without becoming a scald — this happens before anything with hot liquid in it crosses the galley threshold, not on the way out the door with the cart already moving.

title: Read the coffee maker's temperature
instruction: Check the brew temperature gauge before pouring for service.
rationale: A brew that hasn't finished or one running too hot are both a problem this gauge exists to catch before the first cup is ever poured, not after someone downstream says it tasted burnt or felt too hot to hold.

title: Set the cart's wheel brake
instruction: Turn the wheel brake lever to locked before loading the cart.
rationale: A cart with its brake off is a cart that moves on its own the instant the floor tilts even slightly, and locking the brake before loading is what keeps it exactly where it was parked while it's being loaded, not partway down the aisle.

title: Check the cart restraint strap tension
instruction: Hold tension on the restraint strap and confirm it's actually snug against the load.
rationale: A restraint strap that looks clipped in place and one that's actually snug against the load are two different things, and the only way to know the second one is true is to hold real tension against it and feel it hold, not glance at the buckle.

title: Move the cart into service
instruction: Release the brake, then push the cart into the aisle — never the other way round.
rationale: A cart pushed against its own set brake just strains the frame and goes nowhere, and releasing the brake first is what actually lets this cart move where the service needs it, in the order that keeps the frame from taking that strain every single push.

title: Carry the hot-liquid tray level
instruction: Keep the tray level while the aircraft rides through light chop.
rationale: A tray held level is a tray that survives ordinary chop without spilling on anyone, and the only way it stays level is actively correcting for the aircraft's own small movements the whole way down the aisle, not carrying it and hoping.

title: Confirm every cabinet is latched
instruction: Push and confirm each galley cabinet door is fully latched before moving on.
rationale: A cabinet that looks shut and a cabinet that's actually latched are not the same fact, and pushing to confirm the latch caught is the only way to know which one this cabinet actually is before the galley is called secure.

title: Confirm the galley oven is off
instruction: Check the oven switch and confirm it's off before securing for descent.
rationale: An oven left running into descent is a heat source with nobody actively watching it, and confirming it off now is what this galley takes into descent instead of an assumption that somebody else already checked it.

title: Secure the galley for descent
instruction: Latch the cart into its bay, then confirm every cabinet is latched one more time.
rationale: Descent is exactly when a galley that was fine all flight suddenly isn't — securing the cart into its own bay and re-confirming every cabinet is what makes sure nothing that held together in cruise is left to find out the hard way whether it holds together in a descent.

title: Log the galley secure
instruction: Record the galley as secured before returning to your jumpseat.
rationale: The log is the only record that this galley was actually checked and secured on this specific flight — without it, the next crew member through here has no way to know whether this happened or was simply assumed.

situation: The fasten-seatbelt sign illuminates while the cart is still out in the aisle.
instruction: That cart gets braked and stowed right now, service or no service.
missed: The cart stayed out in the aisle after the sign came on. An unbraked, unstowed cart on an aircraft that's about to move is the hazard this entire procedure is built around.

situation: A jolt knocks a capped container loose and hot liquid spills across the galley floor.
instruction: That gets contained before anyone steps in it, not chased down mid-descent.
missed: The spill sat on the galley floor while the closeout continued around it. That is exactly the scald-and-fall combination this station exists to keep off the floor.

explanation: That galley oven is still on. An oven running with nobody actively cooking in it is a heat source this galley has no reason to be carrying into descent, and it gets switched off as part of securing, not left for whoever notices next.

That cart is standing in the aisle with its brake off. An unbraked cart on a moving aircraft does not stay where it was left — it rolls, and a rolling cart loaded with hot liquid and glass is its own hazard before it ever reaches anyone.

That hot-liquid container is sitting uncapped. An uncapped container of anything hot has no business leaving this galley — a cap costs nothing to close and everything to have skipped the one time the aircraft moves without warning.

That galley cabinet door is not latched. An unlatched cabinet at altitude does not stay closed on its own, and whatever is stacked behind it becomes exactly as loose as the door the moment turbulence actually tests it.

title: Pull the disruptive-passenger procedure
instruction: Open the airline's own procedure before approaching the passenger.
rationale: This procedure is what the airline actually trained for exactly this situation — working from it is what keeps every step that follows in the order the airline decided works, not whatever this crew member's own instinct says to try first.

title: Read the situation, then open up space
instruction: Watch for the raised volume and the sharp movements first, then put real space between yourself and them before saying a word.
rationale: A loud voice and quick, sharp movement are simply what this looks like right now — reading them for what they are, without guessing at a cause, is what earns the seconds this crew needs to open up real space before anything gets closer to a confrontation.

title: Scan the area around the seat
instruction: Two things near this seat aren't right. Find them before this goes any further.
rationale: Anything within reach that can be turned into a weapon, and anything blocking the path to the one door this whole response protects, both get caught and fixed now, while there's still time to fix them without a confrontation over it.

title: Alert the other crew members
instruction: Use the discreet crew alert code to bring other flight attendants aware, without announcing anything to the cabin.
rationale: Every other crew member on this aircraft needs to know this is happening without the passenger or the surrounding rows hearing it announced — the discreet code is what makes the whole crew aware without turning one seat's problem into the entire cabin's spectacle.

title: Talk them down before anything else
instruction: Slow your own voice down, say out loud what set them off, then hand them one real option to take.
rationale: Slowing your own pace is the single lever this crew actually has over how fast this keeps escalating, and it tends to drag the other person's pace down along with it — naming what set them off before handing over an option is what keeps that option from landing as being talked down to.

title: Notify the captain
instruction: Call the flight deck and report the situation, in plain factual terms.
rationale: The captain's own decisions from here — whether the flight deck door gets reinforced, whether this flight diverts, whether restraint is ever authorized — all rest on hearing an accurate report now, not being caught up on it after the fact.

title: Reinforce the flight deck door
instruction: Turn the reinforcement lever on the flight deck door per the airline's procedure.
rationale: The flight deck door is what this entire response ultimately protects, and reinforcing it the moment a disturbance is confirmed is what keeps that protection ahead of the situation instead of reacting to it only if things get worse.

title: Confirm the crew alert actually sent
instruction: Read the alert panel and confirm every crew station acknowledged.
rationale: An alert sent and an alert received by every crew station are two different facts, and confirming the second one is what makes sure this crew is actually acting together rather than one person assuming everyone else already knows.

title: Move nearby passengers back
instruction: Direct the passengers in the surrounding rows away from the seat, calmly.
rationale: Everyone else near this seat is a bystander to whatever's happening, not part of it — moving them back is what keeps a one-passenger situation from turning into a crowd standing around it.

title: Stage the restraint kit out of sight
instruction: Move the restraint kit to a staging spot out of the passenger's line of sight — do not open it.
rationale: Staging the kit out of sight is what keeps this crew ready without escalating anything by letting the passenger see it — it stays closed and stays staged until the captain gives an actual answer, not before.

title: Confirm the captain's authorization
instruction: Confirm the captain's explicit authorization before anything about restraint moves forward.
rationale: Whether restraint is ever used is the captain's decision alone, made with the full picture from the flight deck — this crew's job is confirming that explicit word was actually given, never assuming it or acting ahead of it.

title: Log the incident factually
instruction: Record exactly what happened and when — observed facts only, no interpretation.
rationale: This log is what the airline, and potentially law enforcement at the next stop, reads afterward — it holds up only if it says exactly what was observed and when, not what this crew guessed the passenger was thinking.

title: Request a debrief for yourself
instruction: Request a debrief for the crew who handled this, not just an incident form about the passenger.
rationale: An incident report is a record about what the passenger did — a debrief is about what this crew just went through standing at that seat, and it deserves its own line, not an afterthought bolted onto the report.

situation: A passenger two rows back is on their feet, recording video and calling out encouragement at the disruptive passenger.
instruction: Get them back with the rest of the row, not into a conversation about the footage.
missed: The recording and the cheering kept going the whole time, unaddressed. One disruptive seat now has an audience actively feeding it.

situation: The passenger stands and starts moving up the aisle toward the flight deck door.
instruction: That door gets reinforced right now, not after they arrive at it.
missed: The passenger kept moving toward the flight deck door while it sat unreinforced. That is exactly the outcome this entire procedure exists to prevent.

explanation: That card reads "you need to calm down right now." Barking an order at someone already keyed up doesn't settle a single thing — it hands them one more reason to push back harder instead of easing off.

That cart is parked square in the path to the flight deck door. Nothing sits between this crew and the ability to reach and reinforce that door the instant it's needed — a blocked path here is a blocked path to the one door this entire response is built around protecting.

That broken bottle is sitting well within the passenger's own reach. Anything that can be picked up and used to hurt someone gets moved out of reach the moment it's spotted — this is not a detail that waits for the situation to calm down on its own.

That restraint kit is sitting open on a seat back, in plain view, before anyone has decided anything. A restraint kit gets staged out of sight and stays closed until the captain gives an explicit answer — laid out like this, it escalates the exact situation this crew is trying to calm.

title: Read last night's inspection report
instruction: Read the last driver's vehicle inspection report and the mechanic's sign-off for anything they wrote up.
rationale: 49 CFR 396 has a driver review the last inspection report and sign it where defects were repaired, because a defect the last driver wrote up is either fixed and signed for or still there; starting the day without reading it means inheriting a problem blind.

title: Unplug and stow the charge cable, shut the port door
instruction: Unlatch the charge connector, carry the cable back to its hanger, then close the tractor's charge port door.
rationale: A charge cable left connected is pulled from the dispenser when the tractor moves, and an open charge port lets water and road grime into the inlet; stowing both is the first item because it is the one a battery-electric truck adds to the walk-around.

title: Read the state of charge against the day's turns
instruction: Read the charge and estimated range and commit once they settle in the band your turns need, with a margin for queues.
rationale: Terminal queues and traffic both use charge, and a truck that runs short between the terminal and the warehouse becomes a breakdown in a lane; matching the charge to the day's turns, with a margin, is the drayage version of checking the fuel.

title: Look at the orange cables — do not touch
instruction: Look under the cab at the orange high-voltage cables and their clips for damage, and report anything you see.
rationale: The orange cables carry the battery's high voltage and are for qualified technicians only under NFPA 70E, but a driver's eyes on the walk-around are often the first to spot a cable hanging from a broken clip or rubbing on the frame; look, report, never handle.

title: Build air on the electric compressor and hold it
instruction: Run the electric air compressor and keep the pressure inside the band while you watch for leaks.
rationale: A battery-electric tractor's air brakes are fed by an electric compressor instead of an engine-driven one, but 49 CFR 393 air brake requirements are the same; building pressure and watching it hold is how a leak in the lines or a weak compressor is found before the brakes need it.

title: Hold a full brake application
instruction: With the air built, hold a full service brake application and watch the gauge stay steady.
rationale: A full application held for a minute shows whether the brake system leaks under pressure, and on an electric truck it proves the friction brakes on their own, since regenerative braking does much of the everyday slowing and can hide a weak service brake.

title: Check the fifth wheel is locked
instruction: Pull the release handle to test it, then confirm the jaws are closed round the kingpin and the handle is back in.
rationale: The fifth wheel is the only connection between tractor and chassis, and a jaw not fully closed round the kingpin can let a loaded chassis separate on the road; 49 CFR 393 sets the coupling requirements and the driver's look confirms them every trip.

title: Lock the container to the chassis
instruction: Check every chassis twistlock is turned and locked into the container's corner castings.
rationale: A container rides on a chassis held only by its twistlocks, and one left unlocked can let the box shift or lift on a turn; 49 CFR 393 cargo securement covers intermodal containers, and the driver checks the locks each time a box is loaded.

title: Check the pedestrian alert sound
instruction: With the tractor on and rolling slowly in the yard, confirm the pedestrian alert sound is audible from outside.
rationale: An electric drayage tractor is very quiet at terminal speeds, where people on foot are most common, and the alert sound is what lets them hear it coming; a silent truck in a busy yard is a hazard its driver cannot see.

title: Walk the chassis tyres
instruction: Look at every chassis tyre, including the inside duals, for pressure, cuts and tread.
rationale: Chassis come to a driver from a pool and are often the least looked-after part of the rig, and an under-inflated inside dual can overheat and fail on the freeway; finding it at the terminal means a chassis swap instead of a roadside repair.

title: Write your own inspection report
instruction: Write the low chassis tyre and anything else found on today's report, and sign it.
rationale: 49 CFR 396 requires a driver's written report of defects that would affect safe operation, and writing today's up is how the chassis pool and the shop hear about the tyre; the report also shows the tractor was inspected before it left.

title: Call dispatch for a chassis swap
instruction: Radio dispatch: tractor ready, chassis tyre low, need a swap before the first turn.
rationale: Dispatch books the terminal appointment, and a truck that arrives with a defective chassis is turned away or delayed at the gate; calling now gets the swap done before the appointment rather than at it.

situation: A yard spotter has walked behind the tractor to check a chassis number while the compressor runs.
instruction: Sound the horn and wave them clear of the rear before anything else — the gauge can wait.
missed: You kept watching the gauge while the spotter stood behind the tractor; the brake test would have started with them between tractor and chassis.

situation: The dash has popped a battery temperature warning: the pack is too warm for a fast charge at the terminal later.
instruction: Note the warning on the report for the shop — the twistlocks wait.
missed: You finished the twistlocks and forgot the warning; the truck arrived at the terminal charger unable to take the charge its turns depended on.

explanation: You reached up to move the orange cable yourself. High-voltage cables are for qualified technicians only — a driver looks and reports.
You went to pull out with a chassis twistlock unlocked. An unlocked twistlock can let the container shift or lift on a turn.
You went to release the brakes with the charge cable still connected. Driving off pulls the connector and damages the dispenser and cable.
You went straight to the truck without reading last night's report. A defect the last driver wrote up may still be there.

title: Read the range card
instruction: Read the course: the pull-through, the serpentine cones, the alley-dock door and where the spotter stands.
rationale: Reverse is planned forwards. Once the rig is backing, a driver sees two narrow strips of glass and whatever the helper's hands say, so the shape of the cone lane, the pull-up that sets the dock, the side the swing comes from and the helper's standing spot all need settling while you can still look at them straight on, not rediscovered with the tandems already swinging.

title: Agree the hand signals
instruction: Agree the signals with the spotter before you back: stop first, then slow, come back and turn.
rationale: Hand signals are a language two people invent together on the spot, and a language one of them misreads is dangerous, so the vocabulary is rehearsed face to face at the cab door before reverse — halt first, since it outranks everything. Paired with it is a promise that never bends: an unreadable gesture, or a guide who drops out of view, means the wheels stop turning.

title: Pull through to the start
instruction: Pull forward along the range to the serpentine start, checking both mirrors for the cones and the spotter.
rationale: The pull-through sets the rig straight at the start of the cone lane, and a straight start is half of a clean serpentine. Checking both mirrors as you go shows where the cones sit against the trailer and where your spotter has positioned themselves, before the rig is in reverse and those mirrors are all you have.

title: Get out and look
instruction: Get out and walk the backing path. Find what the trailer will hit or what will go wrong on the way.
rationale: Walking the lane on foot beats every camera and mirror fitted to a tractor, because it shows ground level, head height at the building and the space directly astern — what a driver in the seat can never see. A toppled marker, a greasy stain under the drive axles and a lamp arm hanging low over the bay are plain as day from the tarmac and completely hidden once you climb back up.

title: Clear the pallets from the swing
instruction: Drag the pallet stack out of the trailer's swing path to the marked clear spot.
rationale: Timber stacked where the box will pivot is the cheapest obstacle on the whole range to remove and one of the most expensive to strike: splintered pallets under the tandems, a punctured sidewall, a shove into the building. Shifting it takes half a minute before reverse is engaged, and nobody should be moving anything in that zone once the rig is under way.

title: Back the serpentine
instruction: Tap the horn, then back through the cones at idle — left mirror, right mirror, left again — following the spotter.
