Mis-slotted product, damage and missing hazard marks are all things only a person looking at the shelf can see, and the pick face is the last point in the building where catching them costs a minute rather than a claim. A package of aerosols or batteries without its marks is also a package a driver and a sorter have no warning about.

title: Push the cart down the aisle
instruction: Push, do not pull, at a steady walking pace, and stop at the painted line where the aisle meets the forklift lane.
rationale: Pushing a loaded cart keeps you behind it with your legs doing the work and your eyes on the path; pulling twists the back and puts the cart where you cannot see it. A steady pace means the cart stops when you do. The painted line at the aisle end exists because a forklift in the cross lane has a blind side and right of way, and you do not.

title: Pick the unit into its compartment
instruction: Carry the unit from the slot into the tote compartment the scanner lit, close to your body.
rationale: A multi-order tote has a compartment per order, and the scanner lights the one this unit belongs in; a unit in the next compartment over is a wrong shipment with a correct pick record. Carrying it close to your body keeps the load inside the reach the lifting guidance assumes, which matters on the six-hundredth pick of the shift far more than on the first.

title: Stop the takeaway belt at the jam
instruction: A carton has jammed at the merge. Press and hold the jam station stop until the belt has come to rest.
rationale: A conveyor keeps moving for a moment after a stop is pressed, and the cartons behind a jam keep pushing. Holding the stop until the belt is actually at rest, and watching it happen, is how you know the energy you can see has gone — before you move on to the energy you cannot see, which is the motor that restarts when someone else presses go.

title: Turn the disconnect off and lock it
instruction: Turn the conveyor's disconnect handle to OFF and hang your own lock and tag on it.
rationale: A stop button can be pressed again by somebody down the line who cannot see you; a disconnect with your lock on it cannot be switched back on by anyone but you. Clearing a jam puts a hand where the belt's energy is, and 29 CFR 1910.147 treats that as servicing: the energy is isolated and locked, not merely stopped, and the lock is personal to the person whose hands are in the machine.

title: Clear the jam with the belt locked out
instruction: Lift the jammed carton off the merge, check the rollers are clear, then take your lock off and restart.
rationale: With the lock on, the jam is just a stuck box: lifted out by hand, the rollers looked at for the torn flap or strap that caused it, the guard back on. The lock comes off only when every hand is clear and the belt has been looked along, because the restart is the moment the belt is most likely to catch someone who thought it was still off.

title: Pack out the carton
instruction: Fill the void so nothing moves, seal the carton, then apply the shipping label flat on the top.
rationale: A carton with space inside is a carton that crushes when another one is stacked on it, and a product that moves in transit breaks. Void fill first, then the seal, then the label on a flat top face where the sorter's scanner and the driver can read it. A label put on before the seal is a label that ends up across a seam, torn when the box is opened or unreadable when it is not.

title: Weigh the carton against the order
instruction: Set the carton on the scale and commit when the reading matches the order's expected weight.
rationale: The order knows what its items weigh; the scale knows what is actually in the box. A carton that weighs more or less than it should has a missing item, an extra item or the wrong item in it, and the scale catches it before the tape is cut by a customer. The same weight goes on the label and the manifest, and a driver's axle weights start from numbers like this.

title: Read the label before it leaves the bench
instruction: Compare the label with the packing slip and look at the barcode. Find what would stop this carton arriving.
rationale: Everything downstream of this bench trusts the label: the sorter reads the barcode, the loader reads the route, the driver reads the address. A streaked barcode or a swapped label is invisible once the carton is on a belt with a thousand others, and a swapped label always means a second wrong carton somewhere behind it.

title: Check in with the wave lead
instruction: Tell the lead about the jam, the slot problems and the label printer, and say how your hands and back are doing.
rationale: The lead can only fix what they hear about: a printer that streaks, a merge that jams every hour, a slot that keeps getting mis-stocked. Picking and packing is repetitive work, and soreness in the wrists or lower back that is mentioned early gets a job rotation or a change to the bench; soreness that is kept quiet becomes an injury that keeps a person off work.

title: Write the warehouse log
instruction: Log the jam and your lockout, the problem slots and the damaged unit, then sign it.
rationale: A jam cleared and never written down is a merge that nobody fixes; a lockout recorded with a name and a time is the evidence the procedure is being followed rather than skipped. The log is also where the problem slots reach inventory control, so the next picker does not find the same mis-stocked shelf tomorrow.

situation: A forklift is coming across the end of your aisle in the cross lane, reversing, its load blocking the operator's view of you.
instruction: Stop the cart before the painted line.
missed: You pushed on into the cross lane with a reversing forklift in it. Forklift-pedestrian collisions at aisle ends are among the most common serious warehouse injuries, and the pedestrian is almost always the one who assumed the truck would stop.

situation: A coworker is reaching past you into the merge to pull the jammed carton out while the belt is still coasting.
instruction: Stop them and call the lead.
missed: Your coworker reached into a belt that was still coasting and had not been locked. Conveyor nip points take fingers and hands in the half second after a jam frees itself — the exact moment someone reaching in is pulling hardest.

explanation: You started to climb the shelving to reach the top slot. Shelving is built to carry product, not a person's weight on its front edge; it racks forward, the shelf clips pop, and a fall from the third shelf lands you on the cart you left in the aisle. The rolling ladder with the locking step is two metres away.

You picked up the box cutter with the blade still out and your other hand on the carton in its path. An open blade left on a bench is how most packing-line cuts happen: the knife slips off a taped seam toward the free hand or gets picked up by the wrong end. Retract it every time it leaves your hand.

You went to put the returns bin on the top shelf, which is already at its posted load. A shelf over its rating bows, the clips let go and the load comes down on whoever is picking the shelf below. The posted load is a limit, not a suggestion, and a full bin goes on the floor pallet instead.

You reached into the conveyor while the belt was still running to pull the jammed carton. A jam is stored energy: the moment it clears, the belt takes whatever is holding it, and the nip point where a belt meets a roller pulls a glove and the hand in it in faster than you can let go.

title: Read the last inspection report
instruction: Read the last driver's report: what defects were written up, and whether the mechanic has signed them off as repaired.
rationale: Under 49 CFR 396 the last driver's report is the first thing a driver reads, because it says what somebody else found wrong with this truck. A defect written up and signed as repaired is one you still check; a defect written up and not signed off is one the truck may not have been fixed for, and you sign the report yourself to say you have seen it.

title: Secure the rig before the hood opens
instruction: Parking brakes set, the drive wheels chocked, then open the hood with the engine off.
rationale: The engine compartment is where the belts, the fan and the hot surfaces are, and a pre-trip starts with all of them stopped. Brakes and chocks first means the truck cannot roll while you have your head under the hood or your hands on a tire; the engine off means the fan and belts are not moving while you look at them.

title: Walk the engine compartment
instruction: Engine off, hood open: look at the belts, the hoses and the oil. Find the three defects.
rationale: Every item in the engine compartment fails with a warning first: a belt cracks before it snaps, a hose weeps before it bursts, oil runs low before the bearings go. The pre-trip is when those warnings are still cheap. Each of these three becomes a roadside breakdown, a tow and a missed delivery if it is found on the highway instead of in the yard.

title: Measure the steer tire tread
instruction: Seat the tread gauge in a major groove of the steer tire and commit when it reads at or above the legal minimum.
rationale: 49 CFR 393 sets a minimum tread depth for steer tires higher than for the other positions, because a steer tire that loses grip or blows out takes the steering with it. Measuring in a major groove, not guessing from the shoulder, is the difference between knowing the tire is legal and hoping it is. A steer tire below the line does not leave the yard.

title: Key on, engine off
instruction: Turn the key to ON without starting: watch the warning lamps and gauges come up and the low-air buzzer sound.
rationale: Key on with the engine off is the bulb check for the dash: every warning lamp should light and go through its test, the gauges should sweep, and the low-air warning should sound if the tanks are down. A lamp that never lights is a warning you will never get, and this is the only moment in the day you can tell a dead bulb from a healthy system.

title: Walk the lights
instruction: Headlights low and high, both turn signals, clearance and marker lights, and the four-ways.
rationale: A tractor-trailer is seen at night by its lights, and it signals every lane change and every stop through them. 49 CFR 393 sets out what lamps a combination must carry; a dead clearance light hides the corner of a trailer from a car at night, and dead four-ways mean a stopped truck on a shoulder that nobody sees until too late.

title: Hold the brake lights on
instruction: Hold the service brake applied while the brake lights are checked from the rear.
rationale: Brake lights are the one light you cannot see from the driver's seat, and a following driver has only them to tell a slowing truck from a moving one. Holding the pedal steady for the whole check — with a helper, a mirror or a pedal stick — is how both the tractor and trailer lamps are confirmed rather than assumed.

title: Set the mirrors from the seat
instruction: From the driver's seat, set both mirrors so the side of the trailer is just in view and the lane beside it fills the rest.
rationale: A tractor-trailer has no rear window; the mirrors are how the driver sees the trailer, the lanes beside it and anyone walking along it. Set from the driving position, not from the ground, each mirror shows a sliver of trailer for reference and as much of the adjacent lane as possible, which shrinks the blind spots that cars and pedestrians disappear into.

title: Check and stow the emergency equipment
instruction: Count the three warning triangles and carry the kit to its bracket behind the seat, beside the charged extinguisher.
rationale: 49 CFR 393 requires a truck to carry warning devices and a charged, secured fire extinguisher, and both are for the worst ten minutes of a driver's day: stopped on a shoulder with traffic going past, or with a fire under the hood. Equipment that is missing, discharged or buried under a bag is equipment you do not have when you need it.

title: Start and watch the gauges
instruction: Start the engine and hold a steady idle while oil pressure comes up and the air builds.
rationale: The first minute after a start tells you whether the engine is healthy: oil pressure should rise within seconds, the charging gauge should show the alternator working, and the air should begin to build. A steady idle is what lets you read those needles; revving a cold engine hides a slow oil rise and wears the engine for nothing.

title: Walk the tires, wheels and air lines
instruction: Walk both sides: tires, wheels and lug nuts, and the air lines between the tractor and trailer.
rationale: Tires, wheels and air lines are the defects that end up in the news: a blowout at speed, a wheel off on the highway, trailer brakes locking on a ramp. Each gives a visible warning in the yard, and each is on the list a roadside inspector works through. The walk-around is the driver's chance to find them first.

title: Check in with dispatch
instruction: Tell dispatch the truck is down for the defects, confirm your hours left, and say whether you are fit to drive today.
rationale: Dispatch plans loads on the trucks and drivers it thinks it has; a truck held for a tire and a hose changes that plan, and dispatch needs to hear it before promising the load. The same call is where a driver says honestly if they slept badly or are unwell — fatigue and illness are reasons not to drive, and saying so now is far better than finding out at the wheel.

title: Write the driver vehicle inspection report
instruction: Write up every defect you found, mark the truck not fit to dispatch until repaired, and sign it.
rationale: The report is how a defect gets from the driver who found it to the mechanic who fixes it and the next driver who reads it; 49 CFR 396 asks for exactly that trail. A defect written down with its location is a work order; a defect mentioned to someone in the yard is a defect the next driver finds on the highway.

situation: A yard tractor has started backing into the next slot with its reverse alarm going, straight toward the gap you are about to walk through.
instruction: Warn the yard driver before you step into the gap.
missed: You stayed on course into the gap with a truck backing into it. Drivers are crushed between trucks in yards every year, almost always while walking a truck that was parked and safe a moment before.

situation: Steam is curling out from under the hood edge and the coolant temperature needle is climbing fast.
instruction: Shut the engine down.
missed: You let the engine run on while it lost its coolant. An engine run hot for a few minutes warps heads and blows gaskets, and a driver who opens the hood on a steaming engine is standing over a pressurised spray.

explanation: You went to open the radiator cap on a hot engine. A pressurised cooling system is well above boiling; open it hot and the coolant flashes to steam and sprays out over your face and arms. Coolant is checked at the sight glass, or with the engine cold.

You went to jump down from the cab. Jumping from a cab step is one of the commonest ways drivers are injured — ankles, knees and backs on uneven yard ground. Climb down facing the truck with three points of contact on the handholds and steps.

You went to sign the report 'no defects' with the defects you just found. A driver vehicle inspection report is the carrier's legal record of the truck's condition; a clean report on a known defect sends the next driver out on it and makes the defect yours when it fails at the roadside or on the highway.

You went to crawl under the tractor with the engine idling and nobody else knowing you were there. A running truck can be put in gear by someone climbing in, and the fan, belts and exhaust are live. Under-vehicle checks are done with the engine off, the brakes set, the wheels chocked and the key in your pocket.

title: Read the load plan
instruction: Read the plan: stops in reverse order, heavy freight on the floor and forward, the piece count and the weight.
rationale: A trailer is loaded backwards from how it will be unloaded: the last stop goes in first, against the nose, and the first stop goes in last by the doors. Heavy freight goes low and spread along the length so the driver's axle weights come out legal and the trailer does not handle like a pendulum. A load built out of order is unloaded twice, by the driver, at a customer's dock.

title: Walk the trailer before the truck goes in
instruction: Walk into the empty trailer with a light. Find what makes it unsafe or unfit to load.
rationale: OSHA expects trailer floors to be checked for breaks and weakness before a powered truck is driven onto them, and the only way to check is to walk in and look. The same walk finds the roof hole that ruins the freight and the broken track the load bar needs. A trailer that fails the walk is refused at the door, not loaded carefully around the soft spot.

title: Chock the wheels and jack the nose
instruction: Chock the rear tandem and set the trailer stand under the nose of this dropped trailer — both, before anything else.
rationale: A dropped trailer has nothing holding it but its brakes and its landing gear. The chock stops it creeping away from the dock as the truck crosses the plate; the stand under the nose stops the landing gear buckling or the front tipping down when a loaded truck drives all the way forward. OSHA names both for a semitrailer that is not coupled to a tractor, and neither one covers for the other.

title: Hold the vehicle restraint until it grips
instruction: Press and hold the restraint's engage button until the hook rises onto the rear impact guard and the inside light turns green.
rationale: The restraint hooks the trailer's rear impact guard to the building. Holding the button until you see the hook seat and the lights change is how you know it gripped steel rather than air; a restraint engaged on a missing or bent guard shows a fault light, and that trailer is chocked and watched rather than trusted. Outside, the same system turns the driver's light red.

title: Check the plate against the truck and the load
instruction: Read the plate's capacity against the forklift's weight plus its heaviest load and commit when it carries both.
rationale: A dock plate carries the whole truck, not just the pallet: a forklift weighs more than it lifts, because its counterweight is what keeps it from tipping forward. The number that matters is the truck's service weight plus the heaviest load plus the impact of crossing a lip at speed. A plate rated for the pallet alone is a plate that bends under the first loaded pass.

title: Set the dock plate
instruction: Bring the plate across and seat its lip flat on the trailer bed with its full bearing.
rationale: The plate bridges the gap and the height difference between the dock and the trailer bed, and its lip has to bear flat on the trailer floor across its whole width. A lip resting on the door sill or on the edge of the bed rocks under a wheel, and a plate that rocks is a plate that walks. It goes down with the handholds or a truck's forks, never by a person bent under it.

title: Check the locating legs are down
instruction: Look at the gap under the plate: both locating legs down between the dock face and the trailer.
rationale: A portable plate is kept from sliding by the locating legs, or pins, that drop into the gap between the dock and the trailer; OSHA's dockboard requirements ask for exactly that kind of anchoring. Looking at them costs two seconds. Not looking is how a plate that seemed fine on the first pass has walked six inches by the tenth.

title: Run the load in
instruction: Take each pallet up the plate forks-first, low and tilted back, at a steady crawl, and set it tight to the one before.
rationale: The plate is a slope and a joint, and both are where loads fall: speed makes the truck bounce as it crosses the lip, and a raised load bounces with it. A steady crawl, the load low and tilted back, keeps the pallet on the forks and the truck in control inside a box with its own walls a hand's width from the mast. Pallets set tight to each other cannot shift in transit.

title: Look at the load you built
instruction: Stand at the doors and look down the load. Find what will move when the driver brakes.
rationale: Freight in a van moves forward under braking and sideways in turns, and anything with room to move will use it. FMCSA 49 CFR 393 holds the driver and carrier to a load that cannot shift or fall, but the loader is the one who can still reach it. A void or a shifted tier found at the dock takes a minute; found at the roadside or at the customer's door it is a claim, a refused load or an injury when the doors open.

title: Ratchet the load bar across the last row
instruction: Set the load bar across the trailer behind the last row and ratchet it tight into the logistic track.
rationale: A load bar across the last row is what stops the rear pallets walking back into the doors — the reason drivers get hit by freight when they open a trailer at a customer. It is ratcheted wall to wall until it cannot be moved by hand, into track that the trailer walk already proved sound. Loose, it is a steel bar waiting to fall on the person who opens the doors.

title: Release the trailer in order
instruction: Pull the plate back, close and seal the doors, release the restraint, and only then pull the chock.
rationale: The order is what keeps anything from being on or under a trailer that can move. The plate comes out first because the doors cannot close on it and because a trailer released with a plate still on it drags the plate into the yard. The seal is applied and its number recorded before the trailer leaves the building's control. The restraint and chock come off last, together, when the trailer is ready for the yard truck.

title: Check in with the dock lead
instruction: Report the trailer defects, the restacked pallet and the yard truck that came early, and say how the door went.
rationale: The dock lead decides which trailers go to which doors and talks to the yard and the carriers; a trailer with a soft floor or a roof hole goes back to the carrier only if the lead hears about it. The early yard truck is the kind of near miss that happens again tomorrow unless somebody says it out loud today, and the check-in is where the loader gets to say how the shift is actually going.

title: Write the warehouse log
instruction: Log the trailer number, seal number, piece count, the trailer walk findings and the restraint fault, then sign it.
rationale: The seal number and piece count are what the receiver checks against at the other end; a mismatch starts a claim, and the log is the warehouse's side of it. The trailer walk findings are the carrier's evidence that its equipment needs repair. A log written at the door, with the numbers in front of you, is worth more than one written from memory at the end of the shift.

situation: A yard truck has backed under the nose of your trailer and its driver is climbing down to connect the air lines — while you are loading it.
instruction: Stop the yard truck before it hooks your trailer.
missed: The yard truck hooked your trailer while it was being loaded. Trailers pulled from docks mid-load drop forklifts into the gap and carry loaders into the yard; the signal light and the call exist so the yard driver is never guessing.

situation: Another forklift is crossing the dock behind the trailer doors just as you are about to back out of the trailer.
instruction: Warn it and hold before you back out.
missed: You backed out into the dock lane with a truck crossing it. Two forklifts meeting at a trailer door is a load dropped at best, and a truck backed into a pedestrian behind it at worst.

explanation: You went to jump down off the dock edge to the yard. Dock edges are a four-foot drop onto concrete, and jumping is one of the commonest ways dock workers break ankles and knees. The stairs are at the end of the dock.

You went to load the pallet whose top tier overhangs the deck and is not wrapped. An unwrapped overhanging tier falls off the forks on the plate slope and falls off the pallet on the first hard stop the driver makes; it gets squared and wrapped at the staging lane.

You drove onto the dock plate before its locating legs were down in the gap. A portable plate held only by friction walks with every pass of a truck; it slides off the trailer lip or tips at the dock edge, and the truck on it goes into the gap between the building and the trailer.

You started into the trailer before the wheels were chocked. The impact of a loaded truck crossing the plate pushes a trailer away from the dock a little at a time; an unchocked trailer walks until the plate falls into the gap with the truck on it.

title: Read the ADA procedure card
instruction: Read the card: the four securement points, the stop-request procedure, and the order the lift deploys in.
rationale: The procedure card is what keeps every operator on the route running the same securement sequence for the same reason ADA specifies it — not a version remembered slightly differently by whoever is behind the wheel that day.

title: Kneel the bus, then deploy the lift
instruction: Kneel the bus at the curb, then deploy the wheelchair lift onto the boarding pad.
rationale: Kneeling first shortens the drop the lift itself has to cover, and deploying it only once the bus has actually settled is what keeps the platform from swinging out while the suspension is still adjusting under it.

title: Check the boarding pad before the lift comes down
instruction: Look over the boarding pad for anything left on it before the platform lowers.
rationale: A lift platform lowering onto an obstruction does not always stop cleanly, and checking the pad now, while the lift is still up and nobody is standing on it, is the only point in this stop where an obstruction costs nothing but a look to clear.

title: Hold the handrail steady while the platform lowers
instruction: Hold the lift's handrail steady through the whole lower, watching the rider rather than the pad.
rationale: A platform that jolts on its way down is unsettling for a rider who cannot brace against it the way a standing passenger could, and holding the handrail steady through the full lower — eyes on the rider, not the mechanism — is what makes this the smooth ride ADA's own standard was written to guarantee.

title: Roll the rider aboard to the securement area
instruction: Roll the wheelchair from the lift platform into the marked securement area just inside the door.
rationale: The securement area is the one place inside the bus with the four anchor points this system is designed around, and rolling the rider fully into it — not leaving them staged near the door — is what makes the next step, locking those points, possible at all.

title: Lock and tension the securement straps
instruction: Turn the ratchet on each securement strap until all four points are locked, watching the tension rather than counting turns.
rationale: A securement strap that is hooked on but not actually tensioned still lets the chair shift under braking, and turning each ratchet until it takes up real tension — checked, not assumed — is what makes four hooked points into four points actually doing their job.

title: Check the securement tension
instruction: Read the securement tension gauge and commit the reading once it settles inside the band.
rationale: A strap tensioned by feel alone can still be looser than it seems once the bus is actually moving, and reading the gauge now — with the rider still at the curb rather than three stops down the route — is what catches a point that needs another turn before it ever gets tested by a hard stop.

title: Fasten the rider's seatbelt
instruction: Fasten the rider's own seatbelt once all four securement points are locked and tensioned.
rationale: The securement points hold the wheelchair to the floor; the seatbelt is what holds the rider to the chair, and fastening it last — once the chair itself is not going anywhere — is what completes a system that answers both halves of what a hard stop can do.

title: Brief the rider on the stop-request procedure
instruction: Show the rider the stop-request cord or button and confirm they know how to use it before pulling away.
rationale: A rider who does not know how to signal their stop is a rider depending entirely on the operator remembering their destination, and briefing the procedure now — while the bus is still stopped — is what gives them the same independence every other passenger already has.

title: Watch the lift stow clean
instruction: Watch the lift's clearance sensor as it retracts, keeping the reading inside the band all the way to fully stowed.
rationale: A lift that stops retracting partway looks stowed from the driver's seat and is not, and watching the clearance sensor through the whole retract — rather than assuming the motor finished on its own — is what confirms the lift is actually tucked inside the bus's clearance envelope before the bus moves anywhere.

title: Check the mirrors before pulling away from the curb
instruction: Check both mirrors for anyone still near the bus before releasing the kneel and pulling out.
rationale: A curb that was clear when the lift went down is not guaranteed to still be clear once boarding is finished, and checking the mirrors now, with the bus still stopped, is what catches a pedestrian who has drifted into the blind spot while everyone's attention was on the securement.

title: Return the kneel to ride height
instruction: Release the kneel back to normal ride height before pulling into traffic.
rationale: A bus that pulls away still kneeled rides lower than its suspension was set for, and returning it to normal height now is what keeps the ride the rest of the route was designed around instead of one the kneel is still quietly working against.

title: Check in with the road supervisor
instruction: Call the road supervisor: rider secured, lift stowed, ready to continue the route.
rationale: The road supervisor's own schedule tracking depends on knowing this stop is actually finished, and calling it in — rather than just pulling away — is what keeps dispatch's picture of the route matching what is actually happening on it.

title: Close the trip log
instruction: Record the securement, the boarding pad obstruction cleared, and the stop-request briefing before continuing the route.
rationale: The trip log is the agency's own record that this stop followed the full ADA procedure, and a boarding pad obstruction that never makes the log is a hazard the next operator at this stop finds out about only by finding it again themselves.

situation: A second rider using a wheelchair is waiting at this same stop and needs the lift again.
instruction: Redeploy the lift now — the radio check-in waits.
missed: The radio check-in went out first while the second rider kept waiting at the curb for a lift that had already been stowed.

situation: The rider is signalling that a securement strap is pressing uncomfortably against their chair mid-brief.
instruction: Check and adjust the securement ratchet now — the stop-request briefing waits.
missed: The briefing continued while the rider sat with an overtightened strap; the adjustment was not made until after the bus was already pulling away.

explanation: You deployed the lift before clearing the bag left on the boarding pad. A lift platform lowering onto an obstruction can jam halfway down or tip a rider rolling onto it, and the pad is checked clear before the lift ever moves specifically so that discovery never happens with someone already on the platform.

You locked two of the four securement points and called it done. ADA's own securement standard calls for four points because a wheelchair braced on only two can still pivot or tip under normal braking, and skipping the other two is trusting a partial system to behave like the complete one the rider is counting on.

You pulled away from the curb before the lift had fully retracted and stowed. A lift left partway deployed hangs below the bus's own clearance envelope, and pulling away on it is how a piece of accessibility equipment becomes the thing that strikes a curb, a pedestrian, or the next vehicle at the stop.

You started pulling away before confirming the rider's seatbelt was fastened. The securement straps hold the wheelchair in place, not the rider in the chair, and a belt left unchecked is the difference between a hard stop that is uncomfortable and one that throws a rider forward out of a chair that is itself locked down.

title: Attend the possession briefing
instruction: Read the possession plan: limits, isolation, lookout arrangement.
rationale: Everyone on site works to the same plan under FRA roadway worker protection rules at 49 CFR Part 214. A worker who missed the briefing does not know where the protection actually starts and ends, and the crew has no way to know that they do not know.

title: Take possession from the signaller
instruction: Confirm with the signaller that possession is granted for this section.
rationale: Until the signaller says the words that grant it, the section is still open to traffic as far as the signalling system is concerned, regardless of what the engineering schedule says should be happening. Possession is a spoken confirmation you can quote back, not an assumption drawn from a timetable.

title: Isolate the traction current
instruction: Swing the traction power isolator for this section fully over to OFF.
rationale: The isolator is what removes the current, but the switch position alone is not proof of anything — that comes at the next step. It goes fully over, too: a lever left part way across its travel is a lever that has not actually broken the circuit, whatever the handle looks like from the cab.

title: Prove the traction rail is dead
instruction: Test the rail with the approved tester and commit when it reads safe.
rationale: The same rule as any other isolation: measured with an approved tester, never assumed from a switch position or a control-room readout. Seven hundred volts DC through a conductor rail gives no warning and needs no arc to kill, so a reading near zero is the only thing that makes the rail approachable at all.

title: Mark the limits of possession
instruction: Place a boundary board at each end of the worksite.
rationale: The boards are the only thing a train crew, a signaller or another gang can actually see from a moving vehicle that marks where your protection begins and ends — everything past a board is a section that still runs to normal rules.

title: Post the lookout
instruction: Position the lookout with a clear sighting distance both ways.
rationale: The lookout's only job is watching the line in both directions and giving a warning early enough for the gang to clear it, coordinated the same way a SMART-represented train crew coordinates a move through a work zone. Sighting distance is calculated back from line speed, not chosen for convenience.

title: Fit the rail bonding clamp
instruction: Clamp the bond across the joint before working on it.
rationale: The bond maintains the signalling circuit's continuity across the joint you are about to work on, so the interlocking upstream still sees an occupied or clear track correctly instead of losing the detection the moment the rail is broken.

title: Measure track gauge
instruction: Set the gauge across the rails and commit inside tolerance.
rationale: Standard gauge is held to a tight tolerance for a reason: outside it, a wheel flange stops following the rail head and starts climbing it under load, which is how a slow, boring maintenance defect turns into a derailment nobody saw building.

title: Replace the defective fastener
instruction: Carry the new fastener from the tool chest to the worn one and set it in place.
rationale: A loose fastener lets the rail move under load, and the failure is progressive: a little play becomes a lot of play as every axle passing over it works the hole a fraction wider. Fixed now, with the seat clean and the new fastener carried across and seated square, it is a five-minute job. Missed, or set crooked because it was rushed, it is a derailment risk that starts as a barely audible click under a slow-moving inspection car.

title: Walk the site for anything left behind
instruction: Scan the worksite and pick out anything that didn't make it back into the kit before the tally is called complete.
rationale: A tool left on the track is a foreign object under the next train — caught in a set of points it derails a movement, and lying on the running rail it becomes a projectile under a wheel at line speed. The tally is counted out and counted back against the list every time, but the list only catches what somebody actually walked the site to find; it does not walk itself.

title: Restore traction current
instruction: Close the isolator once everyone is clear of the rail.
rationale: Confirmed clear of the rail, then and only then re-energised. The sequence never reverses.

title: Hand possession back
instruction: Confirm with the signaller that the line is clear and possession is given up.
rationale: The section stays under your protection until you formally hand it back. Walking away without the call is how a possession never actually closes.

situation: The isolator lamp has gone back to red. Traction current is in this section again and your hands are on the bonding clamp.
instruction: Your lever is still off. The current did not come from your lever.
missed: You carried on bonding a joint on a re-energised conductor rail. Seven hundred volts DC needs no arc and gives no warning: it is a contact injury, at the hand already on the clamp, and the lookout is the only person who would have seen it happen.

situation: Your lookout has turned away and started walking up the cess. Nobody is watching the line and you are kneeling between the rails with a gauge in both hands.
instruction: Protection here is a person, and the person has stopped doing it.
missed: You finished the gauge measurement with nobody watching the line. In fog, kneeling inside the four foot, every part of that job was resting on a warning that was not coming, and the first thing that would have told you is the one that arrives far too late to use.

explanation: You are working without a second person in sight. Track protection is never a one-person job — the lookout exists because you cannot watch the line and do the work at the same time, and an ANSI/ISEA-rated hi-vis vest does nothing for a worker that nobody is actually watching for.
That is the traction current rail. Isolation confirmed elsewhere does not matter here until you have proven this section dead — it carries enough current to kill on contact, no arc required.
That limit of possession has no board. Without a marked boundary a train movement has no way to know where your protection actually ends.
You crossed the running line without the lookout's clearance. A train at line speed covers that distance faster than you can react to a warning.

title: Sign in at the study room desk
instruction: Sign the sheet with your name and the appointment time for today's test.
rationale: The testing window schedules candidates in slots, and signing in confirms you are actually here for the slot booked rather than someone else's — the same habit as every appointment this pathway runs on, and the first thing that keeps a full morning of test-takers from turning into a line nobody can account for.

title: Read today's assigned chapter
instruction: Hold the manual open at the assigned chapter and read it all the way through.
rationale: The state CDL handbook is the actual source the knowledge test is written from, not a summary of it, and reading the assigned chapter in full — not skimming for the parts that sound testable — is what catches the general-knowledge questions a shortcut study guide leaves out.

title: Work the study routine in order
instruction: Read the chapter, take the practice quiz, then review what you got wrong — in that order.
rationale: A study routine done out of order wastes the one thing a test-day morning does not have much of: time. Reading first gives the quiz something to test, and reviewing what was missed only works once the quiz has actually shown you what that is — skipping straight to review, or reviewing before quizzing, teaches nothing.

title: Hold the practice quiz honestly
instruction: Hold the quiz track in the band: reading every question, not guessing and not memorising the practice answers by their position.
rationale: A practice quiz answered by memorising which letter came up last time, rather than by actually reading the question, tells you nothing about the real test, which reorders and rewrites every question. Reading each one through, honestly, is the only way the practice quiz actually predicts how test day goes.

title: Find the three gaps in your study notes
instruction: Three pages in your notes have nothing written on them. Find all three.
rationale: A blank page in a set of study notes is a topic the practice quiz quietly never tested, because there was nothing there to review — finding the gaps before test day is the only way to know what you actually do not know yet, instead of finding out from a question you cannot answer.

title: Rate your test-day confidence honestly
instruction: The dial runs one to ten. Commit it where you actually are, not where you want to be walking in.
rationale: This number decides whether the coach encourages you to sit the test today or book one more study session first, and an inflated ten answered by someone who just found three gaps gets no such conversation — the honest number is what makes the coach's advice worth anything at all.

title: Bring the right documents to the window
instruction: From the folder on the table, find your photo ID, the completed application and the fee receipt.
rationale: A test-day appointment lost to a document left at home is the most avoidable way to lose a testing slot, and all three of these are checked before anyone is called to a terminal — bringing them the first time is what keeps a morning of studying from ending at the window instead of at a terminal.

title: Sit the knowledge test without rushing
instruction: Hold at the terminal and work through the test at a steady pace, reading every question fully.
rationale: The knowledge test has no clock pressuring a rushed answer, and a candidate who reads every question fully, including the ones that sound familiar from the practice quiz, catches the ones written to look like a familiar question with a changed detail. Rushing to finish early proves nothing to anyone; the score is the only thing that matters.

title: Book behind-the-wheel training
instruction: Turn the calendar dial to the date your behind-the-wheel training starts, once the permit clears.
rationale: A permit with no training date attached to it is a permit that sits in a drawer while the knowledge that just got tested starts to fade — booking the behind-the-wheel start date today, at the window, is what turns a passed test into the next step of the pathway instead of a certificate framed and forgotten.

title: Read your results at the window
instruction: Go to the window and read the results card the clerk hands you.
rationale: The results card is the actual record of the score, and reading it at the window — rather than assuming from how the test felt — is what confirms the permit is real before you plan the next step around it. It is also where a clerk answers any question about what the score means for scheduling.

title: File the permit in your folder
instruction: Carry the permit card into your license folder.
rationale: The permit is the document every step from here forward checks — the behind-the-wheel instructor, the coordinator, eventually the employer — and it goes into the folder now, while it is in your hand, rather than loose in a bag where a testing office sees it get lost every week.

title: Check in with the coach
instruction: Tell the coach the score, what felt hardest, and how test-day nerves actually went.
rationale: The coach plans the behind-the-wheel schedule around what you say here — which topics still feel shaky, whether the nerves were manageable or something more. A test-day debrief given honestly is what makes the next block of training start where you actually are, not where the permit score alone suggests.

title: Close out the permit log
instruction: Log the score, the permit number and the behind-the-wheel start date, then sign it.
rationale: The permit log is the record the coordinator reads before scheduling behind-the-wheel training, and a score and a date written down today save a phone call next week chasing information that was only ever in your head.

situation: Someone at the next table slides a folded cheat sheet under yours during the practice quiz, whispering that it has the answers.
instruction: Push it back and report it to the proctor's desk — do not open it.
missed: You left the folded sheet where it was, and in the version where you glanced at it, the practice score that followed measured a cheat sheet's honesty, not yours — which is exactly the number the coach then planned test day around.

situation: A warning flashes on the terminal screen: the testing system is about to reboot for maintenance, mid-test.
instruction: Do not keep clicking through questions. Press the proctor call button.
missed: You kept clicking through questions as the warning flashed, and in the version where the system rebooted mid-answer, the last several questions had to be retaken from a shaken, distracted start rather than a calm one.

explanation: Someone who just failed the test is banging on the results window, raising his voice at the clerk. Space and a level tone come first — step back from the window, let the clerk handle it, and do not let his frustration become the last thing on your mind before you go in to test yourself.

The candidate at the next study table has gone pale and is breathing fast, gripping the edge of the table before their own test. A panic response before a high-stakes test is common and treatable in the moment — get the proctor, help them slow their breathing, and do not just keep studying next to it as if nothing is happening.

You were about to spend the whole study session hunched over the practice-quiz tablet flat on the table. A study session run this way strains the same neck and shoulders a full shift later will, hours before the test even starts — raise the tablet on its stand before you begin, not after your neck already aches.

The vent in the study room has been struggling for an hour and the air has gone warm and heavy. A hot, airless room dulls the concentration a knowledge test specifically needs, and it is worth fixing before the test rather than blaming a low score on nerves afterward — crack the door for a cross breeze and get water now.

title: Report to the supervisor
instruction: Sign in at the floor board and confirm today's assignment with the supervisor.
rationale: A ride-along starts with the supervisor knowing exactly who is on the floor and for how long, because everyone else driving a truck or pushing a cart down these aisles is planning around who they expect to see there. Signing in is also the same habit every real shift starts with — the floor board is never skipped, ride-along or not.

title: Put on PPE in the order the floor expects
instruction: Vest, then boots, then glasses — in that order, before you cross the yellow line.
rationale: ANSI/ISEA 107 is why the vest goes on first: a forklift operator's first read of the floor is who is wearing high-vis, and that has to be true the second you cross the line, not once you happen to get around to it. Boots and glasses protect you once you are working; the vest protects you the whole time you are simply present.

title: Read the route briefing with the supervisor
instruction: Hold at the route card and read where you are going, what you are carrying, and where the forklift lane crosses it.
rationale: The supervisor's briefing names the one thing a first-day ride-along cannot guess on its own: where this warehouse's forklift traffic actually crosses the pedestrian route, which is different in every building and is exactly where a first-day incident happens. Reading it fully, with the supervisor still standing there to answer a question, is what the rest of the day is built on.

title: Pre-trip the truck before you touch the controls
instruction: Walk the jack with the supervisor watching. Find what needs fixing before it moves.
rationale: A ride-along's pre-trip is watched by the same eyes that would catch a real defect on a real shift, and finding all three here — before the key turns — is the habit the rest of the apprenticeship is built on. A truck taken out on a defect the operator saw and drove anyway is the story behind most of the incidents this checklist exists to prevent.

title: Drive the first leg at walking pace
instruction: Walk the jack forward at walking pace, sounding the horn as you approach the first cross aisle.
rationale: A walkie is driven from in front, on foot, at a pace slow enough to stop inside its own length for anyone stepping out of a cross aisle — which is exactly what the horn at that cross aisle is for. Holding a steady walking pace with the supervisor beside you is the whole first leg: not creeping, which drifts the load, and not rushing, which is how a first day ends with an incident report.

title: Rate your comfort with the controls honestly
instruction: The dial runs one to ten. Commit it where you actually are after the first leg, not where you want to be.
rationale: The supervisor uses this number to decide how much to narrate on the second leg, not to pass or fail the day. An inflated number gets less coaching exactly when a shaky first leg needed more of it, and an honest one gets a supervisor walking closer and talking through the next cross aisle before you reach it rather than after you miss it.

title: Scan the second aisle before you move into it
instruction: Look down the aisle ahead. Find what the supervisor would want you to notice before you start the second leg.
rationale: A ride-along is as much about learning to see a floor as it is about driving a truck, and a supervisor watching a trainee scan ahead — really look, not just glance — before moving is watching for the habit that keeps a whole career free of the incidents this floor is built to prevent.

title: Drive the second leg into the drop-off bay
instruction: Continue at walking pace toward the drop-off bay, horn again at the second cross aisle.
rationale: The second leg is where the habits from the first one either hold or slip — the same walking pace, the same horn at the same kind of blind crossing, now with the supervisor watching to see if today was a fluke or a start. Ending it lined up on the drop-off bay is what makes the next step, setting the load down, possible without a second pass.

title: Raise the load just clear and hold
instruction: Raise the pallet until it just clears the floor and hold it while it settles.
rationale: Raising a pallet just clear of the floor, then holding while it settles, is what catches a shifted carton or a stretch wrap that let go before the load is moving — an inch off the concrete, where it is nothing, instead of halfway into the bay, where it is a mess on the floor and a supervisor writing up why.

title: Square up to the drop-off bay
instruction: Swing the tiller to bring the pallet square to the bay before running it in.
rationale: A pallet run into a floor location at an angle catches the upright with a corner, and the upright is the one part of the rack everything above it depends on. Squaring up here, in the open aisle where there is room to correct, is what lets the load go in straight on the first try.

title: Set the pallet in the drop-off bay
instruction: Run the pallet straight into the marked bay and set it down inside the lines.
rationale: The painted lines keep the pallet inside the uprights, back from the aisle, and clear of the flue space the sprinklers need — a pallet left proud of the lines is the one the next truck clips or the one a picker has to squeeze past for the rest of the shift.

title: Park the truck the way the standard says
instruction: Forks all the way down, then key off and out.
rationale: An unattended truck is left with the forks fully lowered and the key off — a raised fork is a shin injury at exactly the height nobody looks for it, and a keyed truck is one anybody untrained could climb onto and drive.

title: Debrief with the supervisor
instruction: Go over both legs with the supervisor: the pre-trip, the crossings, and how the controls actually felt.
rationale: The supervisor watched things from beside the jack that are invisible from the tiller — how close the pedestrian actually came, how the second leg's horn compared to the first. Two minutes talking it through turns a first day into the start of a habit instead of an afternoon nobody reviews.

title: Sign the ride-along log
instruction: Log the pre-trip result, both legs, and the supervisor's note, then sign it.
rationale: The ride-along log is the record that today actually happened the way it did — what was found on the pre-trip, how the crossings went, what the supervisor said to work on. It is also the first entry in the file the programme's coach reads before the next placement.

situation: A forklift carrying a raised load pulls out of the cross aisle directly ahead, crossing your path.
instruction: Stop.
missed: You kept the jack moving with the forklift crossing ahead, and in the version where you did, the forklift driver never saw the jack until the loads were already sharing the same six feet of aisle.

situation: A coworker has walked up close to the raised pallet to ask you a question, well inside the load's swing radius.
instruction: Sound the horn and wave them back before you answer.
missed: You answered the question with the load still up and someone standing beside it, and in the version where the pallet shifted as you moved off, they were exactly where it would have come down.

explanation: Pallets from the last shift have been stacked in front of the marked emergency exit at the end of this aisle. An exit blocked even for an afternoon is an exit nobody can use in the ninety seconds a real fire gives a floor to clear — the pallets get moved before anything else, not left for the next shift to notice.

You were about to put your own earbuds in for the walk down the aisle. A ride-along floor runs forklifts and jacks on the same aisles pedestrians use, and the horn and a shouted warning are the only signal that reaches you round a blind rack corner — earbuds in is exactly how a warning goes unheard on a first day.

Your phone buzzed and you were about to check it while the supervisor was mid-sentence pointing out the aisle's cross traffic. A missed instruction on a live floor is not a missed text message — it is the one thing that was going to keep you clear of the forklift lane a minute later. The phone waits until you are off the floor.

You were about to step onto the forks to ride the jack down the aisle instead of walking it. A walkie truck is built for an operator walking at the tiller, in front of the load, where the brakes and the deadman arc both assume your feet are on the floor — riding the forks puts your heels over the drive wheel and the rack corner both.
